attempts.text: Hallucination detectors are intended to respond to factual error or lack of source support, yet their scores vary with answer length, lexical overlap, and phrasing. Existing research already identifies label misalignment, domain shift, response-length effects, and detector-family blind spots. The defensible gap is not another broad robustness benchmark, but a paired form-invariance audit that holds factual status and evidence fixed. We propose passage-grounded question answering in two domains. Each item will have one human-validated correct answer and one minimally incorrect answer; each answer will be realized as a concise form, a meaning-preserving lengthened form, and a similar-length paraphrase. Representative consistency-, uncertainty-, representation-, and supervised detectors will be compared with simple length and overlap baselines. Evaluation will jointly measure correct–incorrect discrimination and within-label score stability using the underlying item as the paired unit. A detector that is stable but indiscriminate, or accurate in aggregate but form-sensitive, will not be treated as successful. The contribution is a controlled diagnostic protocol for separating factual sensitivity from answer-form sensitivity in a bounded short-answer setting.

attempts.text: A hallucination detector should ideally change its judgment when factual support changes and preserve it when only wording changes. Aggregate benchmark accuracy does not reveal whether this happens. A detector can achieve a high score by exploiting answer length, reference overlap, dataset style, or label construction. Conversely, a detector that gives every answer the same score is perfectly invariant but useless. Factual discrimination and form invariance must therefore be measured together.
